title: 🧠 EQ Quest: Navigate Life's Challenges
theme: Emotional Intelligence, Social Skills & Mental Wellness
description: Life throws curveballs! Navigate through 10 real-life social scenarios involving bullying, peer pressure, friendship conflicts, exam stress, social media drama, and family expectations. Build your emotional intelligence toolkit -- empathy, self-awareness, assertiveness, and resilience. Your choices shape your mental health and relationships!
learning_objectives: Recognize and manage emotions in yourself and others
Develop strategies for handling bullying and peer pressure
Build assertiveness and conflict resolution skills
Understand the connection between emotional health and well-being

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Read each real-life scenario carefully -- every situation has emotional complexity
Choose from 3-4 options based on your emotional instinct and judgment
Watch how your choice affects Self-Awareness, Empathy, Resilience, Social Skills, Mental Wellness, and Confidence
There are no perfect answers -- some brave choices cost confidence initially but build resilience long-term
Reflect on the feedback after each round to strengthen your emotional intelligence toolkit
tips: The 'easiest' choice is not always the healthiest -- avoidance can lower your resilience over time
Brave choices sometimes feel uncomfortable at first but lead to greater emotional growth
Pay attention to how different emotional skills interact -- empathy can boost social skills, self-awareness builds confidence
Real emotional intelligence means balancing your own needs with the needs of others

player_profile.name: Student navigating teenage life
player_profile.background: Teenager dealing with school, friends, family, and social media

rounds.title: Round 1: First Day at the New School
rounds.story:
Your family just moved to Pune because of Appa's job transfer. Today is your first day at Greenfield Public School, and your stomach is doing somersaults. The classroom is buzzing with chatter -- everyone already has their friend groups, inside jokes, and lunch partners. You're standing at the classroom door, bag clutched tight, when the teacher announces: 'Everyone, this is our new student. Please make them feel welcome.' A few kids glance your way. Some smile politely, others look away. There's an empty seat near the back next to a quiet-looking boy reading a novel, and another near a loud group of kids who seem popular.

Your heart is pounding. You think: 'What if nobody likes me? What if I say something stupid? I miss my old friends so much.' The teacher gestures you inside. 'Go ahead, find a seat.'

Your Self-Awareness: {{self_awareness}}%
Your Confidence: {{confidence}}%

What do you do?
rounds.goal: Navigate social anxiety and take the first step toward making new connections
rounds.setting: New classroom -- unfamiliar faces, unfamiliar corridors

choices.label: Sit Next to the Quiet Boy
choices.description: Walk over to the quiet boy reading near the back. He seems approachable and not part of any intimidating group. You introduce yourself softly: 'Hi, I'm new here. Mind if I sit?' Sometimes the quietest people make the best friends.
choices.feedback: The boy looks up and smiles genuinely. 'I'm Arjun. I was new last year, so I know exactly how you feel.' Over the next week, Arjun shows you around, introduces you to the library, and shares his lunch. You chose connection over popularity, and it paid off. Approaching someone who looked like they could use a friend shows strong empathy -- you recognized a kindred spirit instead of being drawn to surface-level popularity. Building one genuine friendship first creates a safe base from which you can branch out.

choices.label: Sit Near the Popular Group
choices.description: Walk confidently toward the loud, popular group. If you can get in with them early, the rest of school life will be smoother. You flash a smile and say: 'Hey! This seat taken?' Sometimes you have to fake confidence until you feel it.
choices.feedback: The group makes space for you. 'Where are you from? What does your dad do?' They're friendly but sizing you up. Over the next few days, you learn their vibe -- they talk a lot about brands, parties, and who's 'in' or 'out.' You gain quick social access but notice yourself changing how you talk and act to fit in. You're building social skills, but be careful -- the confidence you're feeling depends on their approval, not your own self-worth. Losing yourself to fit in can quietly erode your self-awareness over time.

choices.label: Hang Back and Observe First
choices.description: Take the empty seat quietly without approaching anyone. Watch the classroom dynamics for a few days before making any moves. You want to understand the social landscape before committing. 'I'll figure out who's genuine and who's not before I invest.'
choices.feedback: You sit quietly and spend the first week observing. You notice who's genuinely kind, who gossips, and who bullies the quiet kids. Your social map is excellent. But by week two, people have stopped trying to include you. They think you're standoffish. Your observation skills are sharp -- that's genuine self-awareness -- but isolation feeds anxiety. Understanding the room is valuable, but connection requires risk. Being a permanent observer protects you from rejection but also from belonging. The safest choice isn't always the healthiest one.

choices.label: Ask the Teacher for Help Privately
choices.description: After class, approach the teacher privately. 'Ma'am, I'm feeling really nervous about being new. Is there a buddy system or anyone you'd recommend I talk to?' Asking for help is not weakness -- it's emotional intelligence.
choices.feedback: The teacher smiles warmly. 'I'm glad you told me. Let me pair you with Priya -- she's the class monitor and very kind.' Priya takes you under her wing, introduces you to different friend groups organically, and you never feel forced into any clique. Recognizing your own anxiety and asking for support shows remarkable self-awareness and resilience. Many teens would rather suffer silently than 'look weak.' But seeking help when you need it is one of the strongest things you can do for your mental health. This is emotional regulation in action.

rounds.image_prompt: a bright, colorful classroom filled with lively chatter, students in groups sharing laughter, sunlight streaming through large windows, a nervous new student at the door clutching a backpack
rounds.coaching_moment: Consider how this choice affects your long-term resources, not just the immediate gain.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What tradeoff did this decision reveal? What did you gain, and what did you give up?

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: Round 2: The Embarrassing Photo
rounds.story:
You're scrolling through Instagram before bed when your phone starts buzzing nonstop. Someone from school -- an anonymous account called @greenfield_exposed -- has posted an embarrassing photo of you from the sports day. You had tripped during the relay race and fallen flat, and someone captured the exact moment your face hit the mud. The caption reads: 'New kid's grand entrance 😂 #Fail #WipeOut.' It already has 87 likes and 34 comments. Some comments say 'LOL poor thing' but others are brutal: 'Why did they even let this loser run?' and 'Go back to where you came from.'

Your hands are shaking. Your eyes sting with tears. You feel humiliated, angry, and helpless all at once. Your friend Arjun texts: 'Hey, I saw the post. Are you okay?' Your mom calls from downstairs: 'Dinner's ready!'

Your Mental Wellness: {{mental_wellness}}%
Your Resilience: {{resilience}}%

How do you handle this?
rounds.goal: Develop healthy coping strategies for cyberbullying and online humiliation
rounds.setting: Late evening -- alone in your room, phone screen glowing with cruel comments

choices.label: Tell Your Parents and Report the Account
choices.description: Go downstairs, sit with your parents at dinner, and show them the post. Yes, they might overreact. Yes, it's embarrassing. But you know you can't handle this alone. Then report the account to Instagram. 'I need help with this.'
choices.feedback: Your mom's face goes tight with anger -- not at you, at the bully. Your dad says, 'We'll handle this together.' They help you report the account and screenshot everything as evidence. Next day, they speak to the school counsellor. The account gets taken down within 48 hours. Was it embarrassing to show your parents? Absolutely. But vulnerability with trusted people is not weakness -- it's one of the most powerful emotional regulation strategies. You chose to not suffer alone, and that takes more courage than most adults realize. Your brain was in fight-or-flight mode, and you chose to reach out instead of spiral.

choices.label: Own It with Humor Online
choices.description: Take a deep breath and post your own story: a selfie with the caption 'That relay race mud was actually a free facial 💅 10/10 would faceplant again.' If you laugh at yourself first, they lose the power to hurt you. Turn the narrative around.
choices.feedback: Your post goes semi-viral in school. Kids are impressed -- 'The new kid has guts!' Comments shift from mocking to admiring. Priya reposts it with 'Legend behavior 🔥.' The anonymous account loses its power because you refused to be a victim. This is a powerful resilience strategy called 'reframing' -- you changed the story from humiliation to humor. But here's the nuanced part: make sure you're genuinely okay underneath the humor. Sometimes laughing it off publicly while crying privately just buries the pain. If the humor is authentic, this is brilliant emotional intelligence. If it's a mask, check in with yourself.

choices.label: Try to Find Out Who Did It and Retaliate
choices.description: You're furious. Someone did this deliberately. You start investigating -- checking who was near you during the race, analyzing writing styles of the comments, asking around. When you find out, they'll pay. 'I'll expose THEM and see how they like it.'
choices.feedback: You spend the next three days obsessing over finding the bully. You can't sleep, can't focus in class, and start suspecting everyone. When you finally confront someone you THINK did it (Rohan from Class 10), it turns out he had nothing to do with it. Now you've made an enemy and the real bully is still anonymous. Revenge feels righteous, but it hijacked your emotional regulation completely. Your amygdala -- the brain's alarm system -- took control, and your prefrontal cortex (rational thinking) went offline. This is called 'emotional flooding.' The bully won not because of the photo, but because they got to live rent-free in your head for three days. Anger is valid, but acting from anger rarely leads where you want to go.

choices.label: Delete Social Media and Withdraw
choices.description: Deactivate your Instagram, turn off your phone, and curl up in bed. You don't want to see anyone or talk to anyone. If you disappear from the online world, the problem disappears too. 'I just want to be invisible.'
choices.feedback: The immediate relief of logging off feels good -- like pulling a blanket over your head during a storm. But the storm is still there. At school the next day, people whisper and you have no idea what's being said because you're offline. Arjun tries to check on you but you push him away. By week's end, you're eating lunch alone and the photo incident has evolved into rumors you can't even track. Avoidance is one of the most natural human responses to pain, but it's also one of the most damaging long-term. Every time you withdraw, your brain learns that social situations are dangerous, making future anxiety worse. Psychologists call this 'avoidance reinforcement' -- the temporary relief makes the pattern stronger. You needed to feel safe, but isolation is a false shelter.

rounds.coaching_moment: Think about trade-offs: what are you giving up to get this benefit?

rounds.title: Round 3: The Exam Betrayal
rounds.story:
Mid-term exams are next week and you're stressed but prepared. You've been studying every evening, making flashcards, and solving sample papers. Then your best friend Arjun pulls you aside near the water cooler during break. He looks nervous.

'Listen, I got the Maths paper,' he whispers, glancing around. 'Rohit from Section B -- his uncle works at the printing press. The entire question paper. I'll share it with you tonight. We'll both ace it.'

You're stunned. Arjun has never done anything like this before. He adds: 'Bro, my parents said if I don't get above 90 this time, they're cancelling my summer cricket camp. I NEED this. And you're my best friend -- we do this together or not at all.'

His eyes are pleading. You know the pressure his parents put on him. You also know that if you refuse, he might feel betrayed. But if you accept, everything you've studied honestly feels... worthless.

Your Confidence: {{confidence}}%
Your Empathy: {{empathy}}%

What do you do?
rounds.goal: Navigate peer pressure from a close friend involving academic dishonesty
rounds.setting: School corridor -- whispered conversation near the water cooler

choices.label: Refuse but Support Him Emotionally
choices.description: Look Arjun in the eye and say: 'I can't do this, Arjun. But I hear you -- your parents' pressure is real. Let me help you study tonight instead. We'll crack this paper together, the real way. I'm not judging you for being desperate, but I can't cheat.'
choices.feedback: Arjun's face falls, but something shifts in his eyes -- relief, maybe. 'You really think we can cover everything in one night?' You spend the evening doing an intensive study session together. Arjun scores 78 -- not 90, but earned. His parents aren't thrilled, but he tells you later: 'I would've hated myself if I'd cheated and got caught. Thanks for not letting me.' You showed assertiveness without aggression, and empathy without enabling. That's the golden zone of emotional intelligence -- holding your boundary while still holding space for someone's pain. You didn't abandon your friend OR your values.

choices.label: Accept the Paper -- He Needs You
choices.description: Arjun is your best friend. He's never asked for anything like this. His parents are brutal with expectations. If he loses cricket camp, he'll be devastated. 'Fine, send it. But just this once.' You tell yourself it's loyalty.
choices.feedback: You get the paper. You study it. You walk into the exam knowing every answer. You score 95. But sitting at your desk, writing answers you already know, feels hollow. Your hand moves but your mind is somewhere else -- a quiet, uncomfortable place. When results come out and your parents beam with pride, you can't meet their eyes. Every compliment feels like a small cut. This is what psychologists call 'cognitive dissonance' -- the painful gap between what you believe (honesty matters) and what you did (cheat). The grade is real, but your confidence took a hit because deep down, you know it's not yours. Loyalty to a friend is beautiful, but loyalty that requires you to betray yourself always costs more than it gives.

choices.label: Refuse Angrily -- How Could He Ask?
choices.description: You're genuinely offended. 'Are you serious right now? Cheating? I thought you were better than this. Don't drag me into your mess.' You walk away without looking back. Integrity means cutting off bad influences, even friends.
choices.feedback: You feel righteous walking away. You maintained your integrity. But Arjun's face -- that look of shame mixed with hurt -- stays with you. He avoids you for two weeks. The friendship feels damaged, maybe permanently. He ends up using the leaked paper alone and barely passes because he was too anxious to study properly. When you hear he's struggling, you feel a complicated mix of vindication and guilt. Being right doesn't always mean being kind. You protected your values but demolished someone who was vulnerable. Assertiveness without empathy becomes aggression. Your friend didn't need a judge -- he needed someone who could hold a boundary AND hold his hand. Emotional intelligence requires both firmness and compassion.

choices.label: Anonymously Report the Leaked Paper
choices.description: This is bigger than just you and Arjun. If a paper has leaked, hundreds of students who studied honestly will be affected. You slip an anonymous note under the principal's office door: 'The Maths mid-term paper has been leaked.' This is about fairness for everyone.
choices.feedback: The school cancels the paper and creates a new one. There's uproar -- students who had the leaked paper are furious. An investigation begins. Arjun suspects you and confronts you: 'Was it you? I trusted you!' You deny it, adding another layer of dishonesty to a situation you were trying to make honest. The school system benefited, but your friendship and your own integrity around honesty took a hit. Whistleblowing is sometimes necessary and courageous, but doing it anonymously while lying to your friend's face creates a moral tangle. The 'right thing' done through deception still carries emotional cost. Sometimes ethical action means being brave enough to be transparent about your choices, even when it's hard.

rounds.title: Round 4: When Home Doesn't Feel Safe
rounds.story:
It's 10 PM and you're trying to finish your History assignment when the shouting starts again. Amma and Appa are fighting in the living room. It started about money -- it always starts about money since the transfer -- but now it's turned into something uglier. Amma is crying. Appa is yelling about how 'nobody appreciates his sacrifices.' You hear your younger sister Meera's door close softly -- she's 10, and she's probably covering her ears with her pillow again.

The walls in this apartment are thin. Every word reaches you. 'Maybe we should just separate!' Appa shouts. Your blood runs cold. Amma sobs: 'Is that what you want? Fine!'

Your chest is tight. Your eyes are blurring the History textbook. You feel helpless, scared, angry, and somehow guilty -- like maybe if you'd been a better kid, they wouldn't fight. You know that's irrational, but feelings don't care about logic.

Your Mental Wellness: {{mental_wellness}}%
Your Self-Awareness: {{self_awareness}}%

What do you do?
rounds.goal: Practice emotional regulation when facing family conflict you cannot control
rounds.setting: Your bedroom at night -- parents arguing through the walls

choices.label: Go Comfort Meera First
choices.description: Your sister is only 10. She's more scared than you are. You put down your books, go to her room, and sit with her. 'Hey Meeru, want to listen to music together? Put on your headphones.' You can't fix your parents, but you can be there for your sister.
choices.feedback: You find Meera under her blanket, eyes wide and wet. She grabs your hand immediately. 'Didi/Bhaiya, are Amma and Appa going to get divorced?' You don't lie. 'They're having a hard time. But they both love us. Adults fight sometimes.' You put on her favorite playlist and sit with her until the shouting stops and she falls asleep. That night, you feel exhausted but also something warm -- you couldn't control the storm, but you sheltered someone from it. This is empathy in action -- recognizing that someone else's pain matters too, and choosing to be a source of safety. Psychologically, helping others during distress actually reduces our own stress hormones. You also modeled emotional regulation for Meera -- she'll remember that you stayed calm when things felt scary.

choices.label: Go Out and Ask Them to Stop
choices.description: Walk into the living room and face them directly. 'Amma, Appa, please stop. Meera is crying. I can hear everything. Can you please not do this right now?' Someone has to be the adult, and tonight, it might have to be you.
choices.feedback: You walk out. Both parents freeze mid-sentence. Amma wipes her eyes quickly. Appa's face shifts from anger to shame. 'Beta, go to your room. This is between us.' But the fighting does stop for tonight. In the days after, your parents are more careful about volume, but the tension remains -- just quieter. Here's the complicated truth: you were brave, and you were effective. But you also took on an adult's burden. Children should never have to parent their parents. The emotional cost of being the family peacemaker is real -- it can lead to what psychologists call 'parentification,' where kids become responsible for managing adult emotions. Your courage was admirable, but please know: their relationship is not your responsibility. You needed protection tonight, not the other way around.

choices.label: Put on Headphones, Journal Your Feelings
choices.description: You can't control what's happening outside your door. But you can control what happens inside your mind. Put on noise-cancelling headphones, open your journal, and write everything you're feeling. 'I'm scared. I'm angry. I'm sad. None of this is my fault.'
choices.feedback: You write for thirty minutes straight. Messy, raw, uncensored. 'I hate that I can hear them. I hate that Meera is scared. I hate that I feel guilty when I know it's not my fault.' By the time you stop writing, the tightness in your chest has loosened slightly. You didn't fix anything externally, but you processed your emotions instead of drowning in them. This is textbook emotional regulation -- naming your feelings reduces their intensity. Neuroscience calls it 'affect labeling.' When you write 'I feel scared,' your prefrontal cortex activates and your amygdala calms down. You gave yourself the emotional first aid you needed. The only cost? You didn't check on Meera. Self-care and caring for others can coexist -- remember that.

choices.label: Put Pillow Over Your Head and Ignore It
choices.description: Press the pillow tight against your ears. Turn up the TV volume. Focus on anything else. If you don't acknowledge it, it's not happening. They'll sort it out. They always do. 'This isn't my problem. I have a History assignment due.'
choices.feedback: You bury yourself under blankets and blast music. Eventually the shouting stops and you fall into a fitful sleep. But the next morning, everything feels off. You're irritable, snap at Meera for no reason, and can't concentrate in class. Your body absorbed the stress even though your mind tried to reject it. This is emotional suppression -- different from regulation. Suppression says 'this isn't happening,' while regulation says 'this is happening and I'm going to process it.' Research shows that suppressing emotions doesn't make them go away -- it stores them in your body as tension, irritability, and anxiety. The History assignment? You couldn't focus anyway. Ignoring pain doesn't make it disappear; it just makes it show up sideways.

rounds.title: Round 5: The Bystander's Choice
rounds.story:
Lunch break. You're eating in the cafeteria with your group when you notice something happening two tables away. Vikram -- a big kid from your class known for being a bully -- is standing over Faizal, a quiet, thin boy who wears thick glasses and always sits alone. Vikram grabs Faizal's tiffin box and opens it. 'What's this? Biryani? My favourite!' He takes a handful and shoves it in his mouth while his friends laugh. Faizal sits frozen, eyes fixed on the table.

Then Vikram says loudly: 'Oi Faizal, tell your Ammi her cooking is too good for a loser like you.' More laughter. Faizal's hands are trembling. He doesn't say a word.

You look around. Everyone can see this. A teacher is on the far side of the cafeteria but hasn't noticed. Your friend Priya whispers: 'Just ignore it, don't get involved. Vikram will target you next.' She's probably right. Vikram is twice your size.

Your Empathy: {{empathy}}%
Your Social Skills: {{social_skills}}%

What do you do?
rounds.goal: Navigate the bystander dilemma -- balancing personal safety with moral responsibility
rounds.setting: School cafeteria -- public bullying, everyone watching

choices.label: Walk Over and Stand Up for Faizal
choices.description: Push back your chair and walk to Faizal's table. Look Vikram in the eye. 'Hey Vikram, that's not cool. Give him back his food.' Your voice might shake, but you won't sit here and watch this. Someone has to say something.
choices.feedback: Your legs feel like jelly as you walk over. Vikram turns, surprised. 'Mind your own business, new kid.' But you stand your ground. 'This IS my business. Everyone can see this.' A few other kids nod. Vikram looks around, realizes the audience has shifted, and drops the tiffin with a 'Whatever.' He walks away. Faizal looks at you with something between gratitude and disbelief. Your heart is pounding for an hour afterward. Here's the truth: you were scared, and you did it anyway. That's the definition of courage. Your confidence took a temporary hit because Vikram now knows your face -- but your empathy and resilience grew enormously. Research on bystander intervention shows that ONE person standing up changes the entire group dynamic. You didn't just help Faizal -- you gave permission for others to care.

choices.label: Quietly Go Get the Teacher
choices.description: Don't confront Vikram directly -- that could escalate. Instead, slip away from your table, find the teacher at the far end, and point out what's happening. Let the adult authority handle it. 'Ma'am, Vikram is taking Faizal's food and bullying him.'
choices.feedback: You discreetly approach the duty teacher. She looks over, sees Vikram, and walks over with authority. 'Vikram, my office. NOW.' The situation is defused by someone who has the power to create real consequences. Faizal is safe, and you're not a target. Some people might call this 'snitching,' but that's bully logic designed to protect bullies. What you did is called 'prosocial reporting' -- using the systems that exist to protect people. You assessed the situation, recognized that direct confrontation with someone bigger could be dangerous, and chose the strategic path. This is emotional intelligence meeting practical wisdom. The only caveat: make sure you follow up with Faizal afterward, so he knows someone cared.

choices.label: Don't Intervene Now, but Sit with Faizal After
choices.description: You're not brave enough to confront Vikram right now -- and that's honest. But after Vikram leaves, you'll go sit with Faizal, share your lunch, and make sure he's okay. You can't be a hero, but you can be a friend.
choices.feedback: Vikram finishes his performance and struts away. You pick up your tiffin, walk over to Faizal, and sit down. 'Hey, I'm sorry about that. Here, have some of mine.' Faizal looks at you, stunned that anyone came over. You eat lunch together. He barely speaks, but by the end, there's the ghost of a smile. You didn't stop the bullying, and that might eat at you. But you did something many people never do -- you showed up AFTER the crisis. Psychologists call this 'second-responder support,' and it matters enormously. Victims of bullying often feel invisible. You made Faizal visible. Your self-awareness in recognizing your own fear is healthy, but be careful not to use 'I'm not brave enough' as a permanent excuse. Courage, like a muscle, grows when you use it.

choices.label: Stay Seated -- It's Not Your Problem
choices.description: Priya is right. Getting involved means painting a target on your back. You're new here. You don't fully understand the social dynamics yet. Faizal isn't your friend. It's not personal. 'I'll just keep eating and not make eye contact.'
choices.feedback: You keep your head down and eat. The scene plays out and ends. Vikram leaves. Faizal sits alone, biryani ruined, dignity shattered. Life goes on. But at night, Faizal's trembling hands flash in your mind. You could have done something -- anything -- and you chose comfort over compassion. Here's what research shows: bystanders who do nothing experience guilt, lowered self-esteem, and a gradual numbing of empathy over time. Each time you witness injustice and look away, it becomes easier to look away next time. This is called the 'bystander effect' -- the more people watching, the less responsibility each person feels. But knowing about it doesn't erase the feeling in your stomach. Inaction has consequences too -- not for Vikram or Faizal, but for the person you're becoming.

rounds.title: Round 6: The Comparison Trap
rounds.story:
It's Saturday evening and you're home, studying for Monday's Science test. Your phone lights up with Instagram notifications. You open the app 'just for a second' and fall down the rabbit hole. Neha from your class posted photos from a fancy birthday party at a five-star hotel -- designer outfits, a DJ, photo booth. 47 classmates are there. You weren't invited. Suresh posted his 98% Maths scorecard with the caption 'Hard work pays off 📚🔥.' Priya shared her dance competition trophy. Arjun posted a vacation photo from Goa with his family.

You look around your small apartment. Your study desk with last year's textbooks stacked as a monitor stand. The ceiling fan that wobbles. You think about your own Maths score -- 74%. Decent, but nobody's posting 74% on Instagram.

A heavy feeling settles in your chest. Everyone's life looks so much better, brighter, easier. You feel small, left behind, and suddenly deeply unmotivated to study. 'What's even the point?'

Your Mental Wellness: {{mental_wellness}}%
Your Confidence: {{confidence}}%

What do you do?
rounds.goal: Recognize and combat social comparison, FOMO, and the curated nature of social media
rounds.setting: Saturday evening -- alone in your room, phone glowing with everyone else's highlights

choices.label: Do a Mental Reality Check
choices.description: Pause. Take a breath. Remind yourself: Instagram shows highlight reels, not behind-the-scenes. Neha's parents might fight like yours. Suresh probably didn't post the subject he failed. Nobody posts their bad days. Open your journal and write down three things going well in YOUR life.
choices.feedback: You put the phone face-down and grab your journal. You write: '1. I made a genuine friend in Arjun in a new city. 2. I improved my Maths from 62% last term to 74%. 3. I helped Meera with her school project and she was so happy.' The heavy feeling doesn't vanish, but it loosens. You're practicing what psychologists call 'cognitive restructuring' -- actively challenging distorted thoughts with evidence. Social media triggers a psychological phenomenon called 'upward social comparison,' where we compare our ordinary moments to others' curated best moments. Recognizing this trap is a superpower. Your 74% represents real growth. Suresh's 98% doesn't diminish that. Two truths can coexist: others can succeed AND you can be on your own valid path.

choices.label: Call Arjun and Be Honest About How You Feel
choices.description: Pick up the phone and call Arjun. 'Hey, I know this sounds weird, but I was scrolling Instagram and now I feel terrible about myself. Everyone seems to have it so much better. Am I being stupid?' Vulnerability with a trusted friend can break the isolation spiral.
choices.feedback: Arjun laughs gently. 'Bro, you saw my Goa photos? My parents fought the ENTIRE trip. I literally cried in the hotel bathroom on day two. That sunset selfie? I took it five minutes after a massive argument.' You're both quiet for a moment. Then he adds: 'Nobody posts the real stuff.' You talk for an hour about the gap between Instagram and reality. By the end, you're both laughing. What you did takes real emotional courage -- admitting vulnerability to another person. Most teens (and adults) suffer FOMO silently, assuming they're the only ones who feel inadequate. But research shows that sharing these feelings reduces their power dramatically. Social connection is the antidote to social comparison. You also strengthened your friendship by being real instead of performing.

choices.label: Create Your Own Highlight Reel Post
choices.description: If everyone's posting their best moments, why not you? Find your best photo, add a filter, craft a caption that makes your life look exciting. Post it. Get likes. Feel better. 'Two can play at this game.'
choices.feedback: You spend 40 minutes finding the right photo, the right filter, the right caption. You post it. Likes trickle in -- 12... 23... 31. Each notification gives a tiny dopamine hit. But an hour later, you're refreshing again, anxious about whether it's getting enough engagement. Instead of studying, you spent your evening performing for an audience. This is the social media cycle: feel inadequate, post to compensate, measure worth by likes, feel anxious about engagement, repeat. You just added fuel to the exact fire that was burning you. Psychologists call this 'performative self-presentation' -- curating an image that doesn't match your inner experience. Every like reinforces the idea that your worth depends on others' approval. The real you -- the one with a 74% and a wobbling fan -- is the one who deserves acceptance. Not the filtered version.

choices.label: Keep Scrolling -- Can't Look Away
choices.description: You know it's making you feel worse, but you can't stop. Each new post is a tiny hit of curiosity mixed with pain. 'Just one more... okay, one more after this.' The Science textbook gathers dust. An hour disappears.
choices.feedback: An hour becomes two. Your eyes hurt. Your mood has cratered. Every post confirms the story your brain is telling: everyone is happier, smarter, more popular, more loved. You haven't touched Science. It's 11 PM and you're exhausted, miserable, and now stressed about the test too. This is what researchers call 'doom scrolling' -- the compulsive consumption of content that makes you feel worse. Your brain's reward system (dopamine) keeps you scrolling while your emotional system (serotonin) crashes. It's the digital equivalent of eating junk food when you're sad -- temporary distraction, long-term damage. Social media apps are literally designed by teams of psychologists to keep you scrolling. You're not weak for falling into the trap. But recognizing the trap is the first step to escaping it. Tomorrow, consider setting a screen time limit.

rounds.title: Round 7: The Anxiety Attack
rounds.story:
It's the morning of your Science board exam. You studied well -- genuinely well this time. You know the material. But as you sit at your exam desk and the invigilator distributes the papers, something goes wrong in your body.

Your heart starts racing. Not normal nervousness -- RACING. Your palms are dripping wet. The room feels like it's shrinking. The words on the question paper blur. You read Question 1 three times and can't process it, even though you KNOW the answer. You know you know it. But your brain has frozen.

Your breathing gets shallow and fast. You feel dizzy. The kid next to you is already writing furiously. The clock shows 9:07 AM -- you've been staring at the paper for seven minutes without writing a single word. Your chest hurts. 'Am I having a heart attack? What's happening to me? Everyone will see me fail.'

This is a panic attack. Your body's fight-or-flight system has activated even though there's no physical danger.

Your Mental Wellness: {{mental_wellness}}%
Your Resilience: {{resilience}}%

What do you do?
rounds.goal: Learn to recognize and manage anxiety attacks using grounding techniques
rounds.setting: Exam hall -- papers distributed, clock ticking, body in panic mode

choices.label: Use the 5-4-3-2-1 Grounding Technique
choices.description: You've read about this. Stop trying to read the paper. Put your pen down. Look around the room and silently name: 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch, 3 you can hear, 2 you can smell, 1 you can taste. Ground yourself in the present. The exam can wait two minutes.
choices.feedback: You put your pen down. '5 things I see: the green wall, the ceiling fan, Priya's braid, the clock, my water bottle. 4 things I can touch: the cool desk surface, my uniform fabric, the pen, my wristwatch. 3 sounds: the fan whirring, someone coughing, pages turning. 2 smells: chalk dust, the rubber eraser. 1 taste: the toothpaste from this morning.' By the time you finish, your heart rate has dropped. The words on the paper become words again. You pick up your pen and write 'Q1.' The answers come. You don't ace it, but you complete the paper. This grounding technique works because it pulls your brain out of the amygdala (panic center) and activates your sensory cortex (present-moment awareness). Your body thought it was in danger; you gently told it: 'Look around -- we're safe. It's just an exam.' This is a skill that will serve you for the rest of your life.

choices.label: Force Yourself to Write -- Push Through It
choices.description: Grip the pen tighter. Tell yourself: 'Stop being weak. Just WRITE. You know this. Everyone else is writing. You're wasting time. FORCE IT.' Mind over matter. Willpower conquers everything.
choices.feedback: You force the pen to move. The handwriting is shaky, barely legible. You answer Q1 but can't remember if it's right. Q2 you skip entirely because the panic spikes when you can't recall the formula. You push and push, berating yourself internally: 'Stupid. Everyone else can do this. What's wrong with you?' By the end of the three hours, you've completed maybe 60% of the paper. Your shirt is soaked with sweat. You feel defeated. Willpower has its place, but fighting a panic attack with willpower is like fighting a fire with your bare hands. Your body was in a neurological state where the thinking brain was temporarily offline. Yelling at yourself added shame to panic -- cortisol on top of adrenaline. The answer to a dysregulated nervous system is never 'try harder.' It's 'regulate first, perform second.' Self-compassion is not weakness. It's neuroscience.

choices.label: Raise Your Hand and Ask to Step Out Briefly
choices.description: Raise your hand. Tell the invigilator quietly: 'Ma'am, I'm feeling unwell. Can I please step out for two minutes and get some water?' Go to the bathroom, splash water on your face, breathe deeply, and come back. It's not giving up -- it's resetting.
choices.feedback: The invigilator nods. You walk to the bathroom on shaky legs. You run cold water over your wrists -- a technique that activates the mammalian dive reflex and slows your heart rate. You look at yourself in the mirror. 'You studied for this. You know this material. Your body is scared, but you are safe.' Three deep breaths. You walk back, sit down, and begin writing. You lose five minutes but gain back your entire brain. Asking for help during a crisis is not weakness -- it's emotional intelligence at its most practical. Many students suffer silently through panic attacks, losing marks not because they don't know the material, but because they're too ashamed to acknowledge what's happening. You prioritized your nervous system over your ego, and your exam score reflected that wisdom.

choices.label: Submit Blank Paper and Leave the Hall
choices.description: This is too much. You can't breathe, can't think, can't write. Submit the paper and walk out. You'll deal with the consequences later. Right now, you just need to escape this room. 'I can't do this. I need to get out.'
choices.feedback: You hand in the mostly-blank paper and walk out. The fresh air hits your face and the panic subsides almost immediately -- because you've removed the trigger. But in the hours and days that follow, a new kind of pain replaces the panic: regret, shame, and a deepened fear of exams. Your parents are confused and worried. The school recommends you see a counsellor. Here's what's important to understand: the relief you felt leaving was real, but it was also dangerous. Your brain just learned that 'escape = relief,' which means next time you face exam anxiety, the urge to flee will be even stronger. This is how avoidance patterns become avoidance disorders. The panic was not your fault -- it's a neurological event. But the response of complete withdrawal means you need support. Please talk to someone: a counsellor, a parent, a trusted adult. Panic attacks are treatable, and you don't have to face them alone.

rounds.title: Round 8: 'I Don't Want to Be Here Anymore'
rounds.story:
It's late at night -- 11:30 PM. Your phone buzzes with a message from Priya, your class monitor friend who always seems to have it together. The message reads: 'Hey, are you awake? I need to talk to someone.'

You reply: 'Yeah, what's up?'

What follows shakes you. Priya writes: 'I've been pretending to be okay for months. I cry every night. I feel like nobody actually cares about me -- they just care about the class monitor, the trophy winner, the responsible one. Nobody asks how I am. I'm exhausted. Sometimes I think... everyone would be better off without me. I don't want to be here anymore.'

Your blood goes cold. 'I don't want to be here anymore.' You've heard in school assemblies that this kind of language can mean someone is thinking about self-harm. Priya -- strong, confident Priya -- is telling you she's drowning. And she chose YOU to tell.

Your Empathy: {{empathy}}%
Your Social Skills: {{social_skills}}%

How do you respond?
rounds.goal: Learn how to support a friend showing signs of depression and suicidal ideation
rounds.setting: Late night -- text conversation with a friend in crisis

choices.label: Listen First, Then Help Her Get Professional Support
choices.description: Reply: 'Priya, I'm here. I'm not going anywhere. Thank you for telling me -- that took so much courage. Can you tell me more about what you're feeling?' Listen to everything she says. Then gently: 'I care about you too much to handle this alone. Can we talk to the school counsellor together tomorrow? You don't have to do this by yourself.'
choices.feedback: Priya types for a long time. She tells you about the pressure from her parents to be perfect, the loneliness of always being the 'responsible one,' and the exhaustion of performing happiness. You listen without trying to fix anything. At the end, you say: 'Tomorrow morning, I'll come to your house. We'll go to school together and talk to Ms. Sharma, the counsellor. I'll be right there with you.' Priya resists at first -- 'What if people find out?' -- but you reassure her: 'Counsellors keep things confidential. And getting help is the bravest thing you can do.' You did something extraordinary tonight. You listened without judgment, validated her pain, and then guided her toward professional help. This is the gold standard of peer mental health support: LISTEN, VALIDATE, CONNECT to help. You are not her therapist and shouldn't try to be -- but you were her bridge to getting the support she needs. This could genuinely save her life.

choices.label: Try to Cheer Her Up and Fix the Problem
choices.description: Reply: 'Priya, don't say that! You're amazing! You have so much going for you -- trophies, great grades, everyone loves you! Think positive. Watch a funny movie. Things will look better in the morning, trust me.' You want to make her feel better RIGHT NOW.
choices.feedback: Priya reads your message and goes quiet for ten minutes. Then: 'See, this is exactly what I mean. Nobody actually listens. Everyone just tells me I should be grateful.' She goes offline. You stare at your phone, heart sinking. What went wrong? You meant well, but you did what's called 'toxic positivity' -- dismissing someone's pain by forcing optimism. When someone says 'I'm drowning,' responding with 'But look how nice the ocean is!' doesn't help -- it makes them feel more alone. Listing her achievements actually reinforced the very pressure that's crushing her. She didn't need solutions or cheerleading. She needed to feel HEARD. 'Think positive' is the least helpful thing you can say to someone in genuine distress. Depression is not a perspective problem; it's a mental health condition. Tomorrow, please reach out to her again -- and this time, just listen.

choices.label: Immediately Tell Her Parents Without Her Consent
choices.description: This is too serious for a teenager to handle. Screenshot the conversation and send it to Priya's mom's number (you have it from the class group). Write: 'Aunty, please check on Priya. She sent me these messages tonight.' Priya might be angry, but her safety comes first.
choices.feedback: Priya's mom checks on her immediately. There are tears, a difficult conversation, and an emergency appointment with a psychologist the next day. Priya gets help. But she also texts you the next morning: 'How could you? I trusted you. I will NEVER tell anyone anything ever again.' The friendship shatters. Over the next month, Priya gets professional help and starts healing -- but she doesn't speak to you. This is genuinely one of the hardest dilemmas in peer support. You may have done the right thing for her safety, but the way you did it -- without warning, without her consent, by screenshotting private messages -- broke the trust she placed in you. The ideal approach would have been to tell Priya first: 'I care about you too much to keep this to myself. I think we need to tell an adult. Can we do this together?' Safety always comes first, but involving her in the process preserves both safety AND trust.

choices.label: Panic and Don't Know What to Say
choices.description: Your fingers hover over the keyboard but nothing comes out. 'I don't want to be here anymore' -- what do you even say to that? You're scared of saying the wrong thing. You type and delete twelve different messages. Eventually you just send: 'That's really heavy. I hope you feel better. Good night.' You put the phone down and pull the covers over your head.
choices.feedback: Priya sees 'I hope you feel better. Good night.' and feels the door close. She came to you at her most vulnerable, and you essentially said 'not my problem' -- even though that's not what you meant. You were scared, and that's completely valid. But here's what you need to hear: you don't need to be a therapist. You don't need to have perfect words. Just 'I'm here. I'm listening. Tell me everything' would have been enough. When someone trusts you with their darkness, showing up imperfectly is infinitely better than not showing up at all. If this happens again -- and it might -- remember: you don't need to fix it. You just need to stay on the line and then connect them with a professional. The iCall helpline (9152987821) and Vandrevala Foundation (1860-2662-345) exist for exactly these moments.

rounds.title: Round 9: The Group Project Disaster
rounds.story:
Your EVS teacher assigns a major group project worth 25% of your grade. Your group: you, Arjun (your friend, hardworking), Neha (smart but bossy -- she's already declared herself 'team leader'), and Rohan (does the absolute minimum and copies from the internet). The project is due in two weeks.

Week one: Neha creates a WhatsApp group and immediately assigns tasks without asking anyone's opinion. 'I'll do the presentation. Arjun, do the research. New kid, you do the charts. Rohan, you do the bibliography.' Arjun messages you privately: 'She didn't even ask what we're good at.'

Week two: Rohan has done nothing. His 'bibliography' is clearly AI-generated. Neha is micromanaging everyone and rejected your charts twice ('Too basic. Redo them.'). Arjun is frustrated. You've redone your work three times to meet Neha's standards but she's never satisfied. The deadline is in 3 days.

Tension is boiling. Arjun snaps in the group chat: 'Neha, you're not the teacher. Stop telling everyone what to do.' Neha responds: 'Someone has to lead since nobody else is stepping up.' Rohan sends a laughing emoji.

Your Social Skills: {{social_skills}}%
Your Confidence: {{confidence}}%

How do you handle this group conflict?
rounds.goal: Practice assertiveness, conflict resolution, and teamwork under pressure
rounds.setting: School project -- group chat and in-person tension, deadline approaching

choices.label: Call a Face-to-Face Meeting and Mediate
choices.description: Type in the group: 'Guys, texting is making this worse. Can we meet at the library tomorrow during free period? No phones, just talking. We all want a good grade -- let's figure this out together.' Take the initiative to get everyone in the same room and facilitate a real conversation.
choices.feedback: The meeting is awkward at first. But face-to-face, things shift. You start: 'Let's each say what's frustrating us -- no interrupting.' Neha admits she's controlling because she's scared of getting a bad grade. Arjun says he felt dismissed. Rohan confesses he's struggling with the topic and didn't know how to ask for help. You redistributed tasks based on actual strengths -- Neha does the presentation (she's genuinely good at it), Arjun does content research, you handle data visualization, and Rohan commits to a specific, manageable section with Arjun's help. The project comes together, not perfectly, but genuinely. This is assertive leadership -- not dominating like Neha or withdrawing like Rohan, but creating space where everyone's voice matters. Conflict resolution isn't about who's right; it's about finding a path forward together. You showed that emotional intelligence and project management are the same skill.

choices.label: Stand Up to Neha Directly
choices.description: Message the group: 'Neha, I respect your drive, but you assigned roles without asking anyone. I've redone my charts three times and you keep rejecting them without explaining why. That's not leadership, that's micromanagement. Can we please discuss tasks as a team?'
choices.feedback: Neha is initially defensive: 'I'm just trying to make sure we get a good grade!' But your specific, non-attacking language -- 'I feel' rather than 'you always' -- gives her room to reflect without feeling ambushed. After a tense exchange, she softens: 'Okay, maybe I was too controlling. What do you suggest?' The dynamic improves, though Neha is still a bit prickly. You practiced what psychologists call 'assertive communication' -- expressing your needs clearly without aggression. Notice you said 'that's not leadership' about the behaviour, not 'you're a terrible leader' about the person. This distinction matters enormously. Assertiveness sits between passivity (saying nothing) and aggression (attacking). You found the middle ground. However, you only addressed Neha -- Rohan's free-riding still needs to be tackled as a team.

choices.label: Just Do Everyone's Work Yourself
choices.description: The deadline is in 3 days and the fighting is wasting time. You'll just redo Rohan's bibliography, finalize your charts, and help Arjun with research. You'll lose sleep but the project will be good. 'It's faster if I just do it myself.'
choices.feedback: You pull two consecutive all-nighters. The project is genuinely good. Teacher gives an A-. Neha takes credit in the presentation. Rohan gets the same grade for doing nothing. Arjun feels guilty but relieved. You? You're exhausted, resentful, and got a cold from sleep deprivation. This is a classic 'people-pleaser' pattern. By doing everyone's work, you avoided conflict but taught the group that your boundaries don't exist. Rohan learned that someone will always pick up his slack. Neha learned that micromanaging works because people eventually cave. You sacrificed your health, sleep, and self-respect to avoid discomfort. This pattern -- if unchecked -- follows people into adulthood: overworking, under-asserting, burning out, and resenting others for not appreciating their sacrifice. Your kindness is a strength, but kindness without boundaries is self-destruction.

choices.label: Go to the Teacher and Complain
choices.description: Approach the EVS teacher privately. 'Ma'am, our group isn't working. Neha is micromanaging, Rohan isn't contributing, and Arjun and I are stuck in the middle. Can you either intervene or let me switch groups?'
choices.feedback: The teacher listens and speaks to the group. Neha is mortified -- she feels publicly shamed. Rohan is embarrassed. Arjun wishes you'd tried to solve it as a group first. The teacher's intervention works in the short term -- roles get redistributed fairly. But the group dynamic is now awkward and distrustful. Neha doesn't speak to you for weeks. Going to authority is sometimes necessary, but it should generally be a last resort after you've tried to resolve things within the group. By skipping the attempt to communicate, you sent a message: 'I don't trust any of you to work this out.' In the workplace, this is called going over someone's head -- it solves the task but damages relationships. The exception: if the conflict involves bullying, harassment, or genuinely unsafe dynamics, always escalate. But for regular disagreements, try peer resolution first.

rounds.title: Round 10: The Final Stand
rounds.story:
It's the last week of term. The school is organizing an inter-house debate competition and the topic is: 'Social media does more harm than good for teenagers.' Your house captain, Vikram (yes, the same Vikram from the cafeteria incident), wants to argue that social media is GOOD. He's picked the debating team: himself, Neha, and he wants you as the third speaker.

But here's the problem: you genuinely believe social media does more harm than good. You've experienced the cyberbullying, the FOMO, the comparison trap. Speaking against your own beliefs feels wrong. But Vikram says: 'It doesn't matter what you believe. It's a debate. Just argue whatever side we're assigned. Don't be difficult.'

Arjun, who isn't on the team, says: 'Just do it. It's just a competition. Don't overthink it.' Priya (who's doing much better after starting counselling) messages you: 'You should speak your truth. That takes more courage than winning a trophy.'

The competition is tomorrow. If you refuse, your house loses a speaker and Vikram will make your life miserable. If you participate, you argue against something you deeply believe. If you ask to switch sides, you're going against your house.

Your Confidence: {{confidence}}%
Your Resilience: {{resilience}}%
Your Self-Awareness: {{self_awareness}}%

What do you choose?
rounds.goal: Navigate the tension between conformity and authenticity, and find your own voice
rounds.setting: School debate -- the intersection of peer pressure, personal values, and public speaking

choices.label: Ask to Argue the Side You Believe In
choices.description: Approach the debate coordinator directly: 'Ma'am, I'd like to argue that social media does more harm than good. I have personal experience with this topic and I believe I can make a stronger argument from that side, even if it means representing the opposing team's position.' This means potentially arguing against your own house -- but WITH your own heart.
choices.feedback: The coordinator allows you to be a guest speaker for the opposing side. Vikram is livid: 'Traitor.' But you step up to the podium and deliver the most authentic speech of your life. You talk about the embarrassing photo, the FOMO spiral, the doom scrolling, the way social media nearly convinced you that you weren't enough. The auditorium is silent. Some students have tears in their eyes. You don't win the debate (the judges score technically), but you win something more important: your own voice. After the event, three students come up to you privately and say: 'Thank you. I felt exactly the same way but couldn't say it.' This is what authenticity looks like in action. When you speak from lived experience with vulnerability and conviction, you don't just make an argument -- you give others permission to be honest too. Vikram may be angry now, but people remember courage long after they forget trophies.

choices.label: Debate the Assigned Side -- It's Just a Competition
choices.description: Arjun is right. It's a debate, not a court of law. Debaters argue assigned sides all the time. You'll research the pro-social-media arguments, present them skillfully, and separate your personal views from the task. 'I can hold two perspectives without losing myself.'
choices.feedback: You prepare thoroughly, finding genuine benefits of social media: connection for isolated teens, educational content, creative expression, social movements. You argue the case well. Your house wins. Vikram high-fives you. But afterwards, sitting alone, you feel... hollow. Not terrible, but not fully right either. You performed well but didn't speak your truth. Here's the nuanced view: there's genuine value in being able to argue multiple perspectives -- it builds empathy and intellectual flexibility. Professional debaters do this all the time. But there's a difference between 'I CAN argue both sides' and 'I'm silencing myself because I'm afraid of consequences.' Check which one it was. If you argued the other side out of intellectual curiosity, that's growth. If you did it to avoid Vikram's anger, that's people-pleasing dressed up as open-mindedness. Only you know the real answer.

choices.label: Refuse to Participate Entirely
choices.description: Tell Vikram: 'I'm not doing the debate. Find someone else.' You don't want to argue against your beliefs, but you also don't want the drama of switching sides. Just opt out entirely. Remove yourself from the situation.
choices.feedback: Vikram scrambles to find a replacement. He's furious. Your house team is weaker and loses the debate. Several classmates are annoyed: 'You could have just helped.' You feel relieved in the moment but unsettled afterward. You avoided discomfort, but you also avoided an opportunity. Opting out is sometimes wise -- when the situation is toxic or harmful. But this was a chance to practice public speaking, engage with complex ideas, or even take a courageous stand. Instead, you chose the path of least resistance, which is also the path of least growth. Every time we avoid something uncomfortable, we reinforce the belief that we can't handle it. Resilience comes from leaning INTO discomfort, not away from it. The question to ask yourself: did you refuse out of principle, or out of fear? The honest answer determines whether this was wisdom or avoidance.

choices.label: Participate but Subtly Include Your Real Views
choices.description: Join the team as assigned, but weave your genuine concerns INTO the argument. 'Social media is good WHEN used mindfully... but here's what happens when it's not.' Technically support the assigned position while making sure the audience hears the real story. Play both sides.
choices.feedback: You deliver a speech that's technically pro-social-media but keeps circling back to 'responsible usage' and 'awareness of risks.' The judges notice the nuance. Vikram notices too -- he's not sure whether to be impressed or annoyed. The audience gets a more complex, honest picture than a standard debate usually provides. You didn't fully commit to either authenticity or conformity -- you found a middle path. This is diplomatically skillful. In many real-life situations, this kind of nuanced positioning is the most effective approach. But be honest with yourself: was this strategic intelligence, or was it hedging because you weren't brave enough to fully commit to either path? There's wisdom in balance, but there's also a version of 'playing both sides' that means you never truly stand for anything. As you grow older, there will be moments when the middle path won't exist -- and you'll need to choose. Practice choosing now, while the stakes are low.

glossary_terms.definition: The ability to recognize, understand, manage, and effectively use emotions in yourself and in your interactions with others. Unlike IQ, EQ can be developed and strengthened throughout life. It includes four core skills: self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and relationship management.
glossary_terms.example: When Arjun pressures you to cheat and you refuse firmly but kindly -- recognizing his desperation (social awareness), managing your own discomfort (self-management), and offering to help him study instead (relationship management) -- that's EQ in action.

glossary_terms.definition: The ability to express your thoughts, feelings, and needs directly and respectfully, without being passive (suppressing yourself) or aggressive (attacking others). Assertiveness is the healthy middle ground where you honour both your own boundaries and the other person's dignity.
glossary_terms.example: Telling Neha in the group project: 'I respect your drive, but rejecting my work three times without explaining why isn't helpful. Let's discuss what specifically needs to change.' This is assertive -- direct, specific, respectful, and solution-oriented.

glossary_terms.definition: The ability to understand and share the feelings of another person -- to mentally step into their shoes and experience the world from their perspective. Empathy has two components: cognitive empathy (understanding what someone feels) and affective empathy (feeling what they feel). Both are essential for healthy relationships.
glossary_terms.example: When Priya tells you she's struggling and you resist the urge to say 'think positive' and instead say 'tell me more about what you're going through' -- you're choosing empathetic listening over problem-solving. You're prioritizing her emotional experience over your discomfort.

glossary_terms.definition: A set of practical psychological strategies based on the idea that our thoughts, feelings, and behaviours are interconnected. By identifying and challenging unhelpful thought patterns (like 'everyone's life is better than mine'), we can change how we feel and act. CBT techniques include cognitive restructuring, grounding exercises, journaling, and behavioural experiments.
glossary_terms.example: During the social media FOMO spiral, doing a 'reality check' by writing down evidence against the thought 'everyone is happier than me' is a CBT technique called cognitive restructuring. The 5-4-3-2-1 grounding technique used during the exam panic attack is another CBT-based strategy.

glossary_terms.definition: The belief that abilities, intelligence, and emotional skills can be developed through effort, learning, and persistence -- as opposed to a 'fixed mindset' that believes these traits are permanent and unchangeable. A growth mindset transforms failures from evidence of inadequacy into opportunities for learning.
glossary_terms.example: Getting a 74% in Maths and thinking 'I improved from 62% -- my effort is working' (growth mindset) versus 'Suresh got 98% so I'm just not smart' (fixed mindset). The same score, two completely different emotional outcomes. Growth mindset protects mental wellness by decoupling self-worth from performance.
